result.tail:
Greek / skyr 
     Strained. Thicker, with less whey. 
     Kefir 
     A drinkable ferment with a wider mix of cultures. 
     Greek 
     Yogurt strained to remove whey, which leaves it thicker. 
     Plain 
     No added sugar or flavoring. 
     Plain means no added sugar, so sweeten it at home with fruit or honey. 
     Plain still lists sugar, and it is lactose. On plain, the sugar line is the milk’s own. On flavored, it is lactose plus what was added. Only the added-sugars line separates the two. 
     ‘Light’ means a high-intensity sweetener. Sucralose or similar stands in for the sugar; the cup is not plainer, only sweetened differently. 
     Fruit-on-the-bottom and drinkable yogurts can run higher in sugar than the pre-mixed cup. Drinkables are made by adding water and flavors. 
     A shelf-stable tub outside the cold case was heat-treated. It is yogurt, and nothing in it is alive. 
     ‘Made with live cultures’ is a past-tense claim. The seal is the present-tense one. 
     The live cultures have to appear in the ingredient list. A tub that names none was heat-processed after fermenting or never held them. The seal is voluntary, so its absence alone proves nothing. 
     Some non-dairy yogurts skip the live cultures entirely. Same aisle, same word on the lid, no ferment. 
     Greek means strained, so the yogurt is thicker and holds less whey. 
     100% grass-fed on the tub means the cows ate grass and hay, never grain. 
     Skip flavored and fruit-on-the-bottom tubs; that is where the added sugar is. 
     Plain still lists sugar, and it is lactose, the milk’s own. On flavored, it is lactose plus what was added, so only the added-sugars line separates the two. ‘Light’ means a high-intensity sweetener like sucralose, not a plainer cup. Fruit-on-the-bottom and drinkable yogurts can run higher in sugar than the pre-mixed cup. 
     If you can’t get 100% grass-fed Greek yogurt: plain organic whole-milk yogurt.
